content: 1. Chronic Low Back Pain and SNRI Antidepressants Studies involving adults with chronic low back pain, with mean ages ranging from 45 to 58 years, have evaluated the efficacy of serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). The antidepressants studied included paroxetine (20–30 mg/day), milnacipran (up to 200 mg/day), and duloxetine (up to 120 mg/day). A crossover trial reported only group-level data, which was analyzed using the same methodology as parallel studies. Imprecision was noted, and the evidence was downgraded by one level due to the pooled estimate crossing the null and the threshold for a small effect. 2. Chronic Low Back Pain and TCA Antidepressants Two parallel trials conducted in the USA (Atkinson 1998, Atkinson 1999) included adults with chronic low back pain, with mean ages of 46–49 years. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) studied included nortriptyline (up to 100 mg/day) and maprotiline (up to 150 mg/day). Another parallel trial (Dickens 2000) conducted in the UK involved adults with a mean age of 45 years and evaluated paroxetine (20 mg/day). Inconsistency was noted due to the limited number of studies, and imprecision was downgraded by two levels because the study included fewer than 100 participants. 3. Crossover and Parallel Trials with TCAs Two parallel trials (Atkinson 1998, Pheasant 1983) conducted in the USA included adults with chronic low back pain, with mean ages of 46–47 years. The TCAs studied were nortriptyline (up to 100 mg/day) and amitriptyline (up to 150 mg/day). A crossover trial (Schukro 2016) conducted in Austria included adults with a mean age of 58 years. This trial reported only group-level data, analyzed similarly to parallel studies. 4. SNRI Antidepressants in High-Income Countries Two parallel trials (Dickens 2000, NCT01225068) and one crossover trial (Schukro 2016) were conducted in high-income countries, involving adults with chronic low back pain and mean ages of 37–58 years. The SNRIs studied included paroxetine (20 mg/day), milnacipran (up to 200 mg/day), and duloxetine (60 mg/day). The crossover trial reported only group-level data, analyzed in the same manner as parallel studies. 5. Imprecision and Inconsistency in Evidence Imprecision was noted in several analyses, with evidence downgraded by one or two levels due to small sample sizes (fewer than 100 participants) or the absence of pooled estimates. Inconsistency was also downgraded when only one study was available, making it impossible to assess consistency. 6. Anticonvulsants for Chronic Low Back Pain Studies on anticonvulsants, including gabapentin and topiramate, were conducted in high-income countries. One parallel trial (Muehlbacher 2006) and one crossover trial (McCleane 2000) involved adults with mean ages of 42–49 years. Gabapentin was administered at individualized dosages (15 mg/kg to the nearest 300 mg), while topiramate was given at doses up to 300 mg/day. Imprecision was noted, and evidence was downgraded due to small sample sizes and the lack of pooled estimates. 7. Gabapentin in Ireland A crossover trial (McCleane 2000) conducted in Ireland included adults with chronic low back pain, with a mean age of 42 years. Gabapentin was administered at individualized dosages (15 mg/kg to the nearest 300 mg). Another parallel trial (McCleane 2001) in Ireland involved adults with a mean age of 44 years, using gabapentin at doses up to 1200 mg/day. Imprecision was noted, and evidence was downgraded due to the small number of participants. 8. Certainty of Evidence and Limitations Across the studies, the certainty of evidence was frequently downgraded due to imprecision, inconsistency, and risk of bias. Many trials had small sample sizes, and some reported only group-level data, limiting the ability to draw robust conclusions. This version maintains the detailed information while presenting it in a clear, professional manner suitable for a medical audience.
